opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think people tend to imagine the main difficulty is just compute, that you need more GPUs and that's it. Compute matters, of course, but at the trillion-parameter scale the hard part is that everything that was "good enough" at smaller scales starts to break, and it breaks in ways that are expensive to discover.

The first thing is **training stability**. A 1T model, especially a sparse MoE model, has many more ways to go wrong: loss spikes, experts collapsing, routing becoming imbalanced, attention logits blowing up. At small scale you can rerun an experiment over a weekend. At this scale a single divergence can cost you days of cluster time, and sometimes you only see the problem hundreds of billions of tokens later. So much of the work is building monitoring and intervention mechanisms, and being disciplined about which architectural or optimizer changes you trust enough to bet a run on.

The second is **infrastructure and efficiency**. When you have thousands of accelerators running for months, hardware failures are not exceptions, they're the normal state. You need fast checkpointing, fault tolerance, and good overlap of communication and computation, especially for expert parallelism, where all-to-all communication can easily eat your throughput. A few percentage points of MFU translate into very real money and time.

The third, which I think is underrated, is **data**. A trillion-parameter model is hungry. If your data quality is uneven, the model will happily memorize the noise. So the data pipeline, deduplication, filtering, the mixture across code, math, multilingual text, and the curriculum over time, becomes as important as the model design itself. And you can't cleanly A/B test data decisions at full scale, so you rely on small-scale proxies and hope they transfer, which they don't always do.

Finally, there's an **organizational challenge**. At this scale you can't have one genius tuning everything. You need infra, data, algorithm, and evaluation people working very tightly together and making decisions quickly under uncertainty. In my experience, the teams that do well aren't necessarily the ones with the most resources. They're the ones that iterate fastest at small scale, understand the scaling behavior deeply, and then have the courage to commit when it's time to go big.

r001.rationale: The response says uneven data can lead the model to memorize noise; it does not suggest larger models tolerate dirtier data better.

r002.rationale: It mentions loss spikes and expert collapse, but does not explain that a loss spike can cause an expert to stop receiving tokens after a parameter update.

r003.rationale: It lists instability symptoms but does not identify differences in numerical scale between layer outputs as a possible cause.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention LoRA or suppressing excessively large values.

r005.rationale: The response does not recommend relaxing clipping after training reaches a steady state.

r006.rationale: It calls for close coordination across infrastructure, data, algorithm, and evaluation teams; it does not suggest a few key people in a small team are more efficient than cross-team collaboration at a large company.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When people hear "a trillion parameters," they usually imagine the hard part is just scale, that you take what works at 100 billion and multiply. But honestly, the challenges change in kind, not just in degree.

The first one is data. At that scale, the model is hungry enough that high-quality tokens become the real bottleneck, not compute. You can't just scrape more; you have to think very carefully about the mix, how much synthetic data you can trust, and how to avoid the model spending capacity memorizing noise. A trillion-parameter model trained on mediocre data is an expensive way to get a mediocre model.

The second is training stability. Loss spikes, gradient blowups, numerical issues with low precision, these things that are an annoyance at smaller scale become existential at larger scale, because every failed run costs you weeks and an enormous amount of money. So a lot of the work is actually engineering discipline: scaling laws you actually trust, careful hyperparameter transfer from smaller proxies, checkpointing strategies, monitoring so you catch problems in hours rather than days.

The third is architecture and systems co-design. Most people training at this size use mixture-of-experts, because dense trillion-parameter training is simply not economical. But MoE brings its own problems: load balancing across experts, communication overhead, routing collapse. You end up with parallelism across thousands of accelerators where the network, the memory hierarchy, and the model structure all have to be designed together. The algorithm researchers and the infrastructure engineers can't work in separate rooms anymore.

And then there's a quieter challenge that I think gets underestimated: knowing whether it's actually working. Evaluation at this frontier is hard. Benchmarks saturate, contamination is everywhere, and the capabilities you care about most are often the hardest to measure. You can burn months of compute and only realize late that the thing you were optimizing wasn't the thing that mattered.

So if I had to summarize: the model is big, but the real difficulty is that every mistake is also big. The margin for error shrinks as the scale grows.

r003.rationale: It mentions numerical issues as a stability challenge but does not identify large differences in numerical scale between layer outputs as a possible cause.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention LoRA or say that suppressing excessively large values with it harms performance.

r005.rationale: The response does not recommend relaxing stability-related clipping after training reaches a steady state.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to clarify is whether we mean a dense one-trillion-parameter model or a mixture-of-experts model with one trillion total parameters. Those are very different workloads, because an MoE model activates only part of its parameters for each token.

At that scale, the challenge is making the entire training system work efficiently. Model states have to be distributed across many devices, and the way you combine parallelism, memory management, and communication determines how much useful computation you actually get. For MoE, expert load balancing and the communication needed to route tokens become especially important.

Then there’s stability. A small numerical issue or a hardware failure can become very expensive during a large training run. You need good monitoring, reliable checkpoints, and a way to diagnose problems quickly.

And finally, there’s the data. Increasing parameter count alone doesn’t guarantee a better model. You need enough high-quality data and a well-chosen training recipe to make that capacity useful. So I would frame it as a joint problem of architecture, infrastructure, and data, rather than simply finding enough GPUs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is making the whole training system work efficiently and reliably at that scale. It’s not just a question of having enough GPUs.

First, there’s memory and communication. A trillion parameters, together with gradients, optimizer states, and activations, won’t fit on one device, so you need to distribute the training. The challenge is choosing how to split the work so that GPUs spend their time computing rather than waiting for data from one another.

Second, there’s stability. A small numerical issue or a hardware failure can become very expensive during a long training run. You need good monitoring, checkpointing, and recovery, as well as careful choices about initialization, precision, and optimization.

And then there’s data. Increasing the parameter count doesn’t automatically improve the model. You need enough high-quality data and a way to test your decisions at smaller scales before committing to a very expensive run. For me, the central challenge is coordinating all of those pieces—model architecture, data, optimization, and infrastructure.
